entries.text: Michigan wants one, and Arkansas, and they say Michigan and Ohio nearly went to war this spring over a strip of land at Toledo. Imagine it: two states fighting over a swamp. Out here we would sell them a better swamp for less.

levels.8-10: Michigan wants a star, and so does Arkansas. They say Michigan and Ohio almost went to war this spring. They fought over a strip of land at Toledo. Think of it: two states fighting over a swamp! Out here we would sell them a better swamp, and for less.

entries.text: Some do. A private needs his captain's leave and he will not get it unless the girl can wash for the company. There are more men in this town than women by three to one, so a girl can choose, and she does not choose a private at six dollars a month if she can get a carpenter.

levels.8-10: Some do. A soldier needs his captain's okay, and he won't get it unless the girl can wash clothes for the company. There are three men in this town for every woman. So a girl can choose. She won't pick a soldier who earns six dollars a month if she can get a carpenter.

entries.text: There is a girl at the boarding house on Lake Street who gives me an extra potato. That is all I am saying. In Chicago an extra potato is practically a proposal.

levels.8-10: There is a girl at the rooming house on Lake Street who gives me an extra potato. That is all I am saying. In Chicago an extra potato is almost a marriage offer.

entries.text: A boy of sixteen from Ohio and a fifer who used to be a sailor. They play the calls all day and the town knows every one: reveille, breakfast, drill, dinner, retreat, tattoo. A merchant on Water Street told me he does not need a clock any more, he has the fort.

levels.8-10: A boy of sixteen from Ohio plays the drum. A man who used to be a sailor plays the fife. They play the calls all day, and the town knows every one. There is a call to wake up, to eat, to march, to eat again, to end the day, and to go to bed. A store owner on Water Street told me he does not need a clock anymore. He has the fort.

entries.text: Strange. I have a commission, a sword, and a company of men who would rather be carpenters. The town invites me to every supper and every ball because an officer in a blue coat makes a room look respectable. The rest of the time I write reports nobody reads.

levels.8-10: It is strange. I am an officer. I have a sword and a group of men who would rather be carpenters. The town asks me to every supper and every dance. A man in a blue army coat makes a room look proper. The rest of the time I write reports nobody reads.

entries.text: People have come from all the villages for the payment, for the money and the goods the treaty promised. They say it will be soon. We have been waiting a long time. While we wait, the whiskey sellers come to the camps every night, and the traders come with their books to say what everybody owes.

levels.8-10: People have come from all the villages for the payment. That is the money and goods the treaty promised. They say it will come soon. We have waited a long time. While we wait, the whiskey sellers come to the camps every night. The traders come with their books to say what everybody owes.

entries.text: Shabbona, of the Ottawa and Potawatomi, from the Fox River country. In the Black Hawk war he rode through the settlements day and night to warn the settlers that Black Hawk's men were coming, and many lived because of him. Some of our own people have never forgiven him.

levels.8-10: Shabbona, of the Ottawa and Potawatomi, from the Fox River land. In the Black Hawk war he rode day and night through the farms. He warned the settlers that Black Hawk's men were coming. Many lived because of him. Some of our own people have never forgiven him.

entries.text: Twenty years with the brigades, from Mackinac to the Illinois, paddling and carrying and singing. A voyageur's back is gone at forty, but his voice is the last thing to go. Now I work for Colonel Beaubien and sing in the evenings outside his door.

levels.8-10: Yes, for twenty years, from Mackinac to the Illinois River. I paddled, carried and sang. A canoe man's back is worn out by forty, but his voice is the last thing to go. Now I work for Colonel Beaubien. In the evenings I sing outside his door.

entries.text: Jean Baptiste Beaubien, a militia colonel and the oldest trader in the town, after the Kinzies. He has two families and twenty children and the whole fort reservation, if the government lets him keep it. He is the most generous man in Chicago and the noisiest. Go and see him. He will kiss you on both cheeks.

levels.8-10: Jean Baptiste Beaubien. He leads the town's soldiers, and after the Kinzies he is the oldest trader in town. He has two families and twenty children. He owns all the fort's land too, if the government lets him keep it. He is the kindest man in Chicago, and the loudest. Go and see him. He will kiss you on both cheeks.

entries.text: I like the people. Every woman in this town came from somewhere else and left somebody behind, so we look after each other. Mrs. Kinzie, the agent's wife, came out in thirty-one and wrote home that it was a wilderness, and now she gives the best suppers in Chicago. Go and see her. She will tell you how she crossed the prairie in winter on horseback.

levels.8-10: I like the people. Every woman in this town came from somewhere else and left somebody behind. So we look after each other. Mrs. Kinzie came out in 1831. She wrote home that it was a wilderness. Now she gives the best suppers in Chicago. Go and see her. She will tell you how she rode across the prairie in winter.

entries.text: Everything comes on a boat and the boat sets the price. Flour twelve dollars the barrel this spring, when the boats were late; eggs dear; butter dearer, and half of it rancid by the time it gets here. A woman with a cow and a hen yard is a rich woman, whatever her husband is.

levels.8-10: Everything comes on a boat, and the boat sets the price. This spring the boats were late, and flour cost twelve dollars a barrel. Eggs cost a lot. Butter cost more, and half of it was spoiled by the time it got here. A woman with a cow and some hens is a rich woman, whatever her husband is.

entries.text: Calico, tea, sugar, candles, pins, and whatever the store has that it did not have last week. Mr. Gale has books and paper and, once, a parcel of Boston magazines that every lady in town read in a single week and passed round until they fell apart. levels.8-10: Cotton cloth, tea, sugar, candles, pins, and anything the store has that it did not have last week. Mr. Gale sells books and paper. Once he had a bundle of Boston magazines. entries.text: Carry the water from the river or the lake, heat it in a copper over the fire, scrub on a board with soft soap, rinse, wring, and hang it out where the mud will not splash it, which is nowhere. Monday is wash day. Monday is also when everybody's husband brings home the mud of a week.

levels.8-10: You carry water from the river or the lake. You heat it in a big pot over the fire. You scrub the clothes on a board with soft soap. Then you rinse them, squeeze them out, and hang them where the mud won't splash them. There is no such place! Monday is wash day. Monday is also when every husband brings home a week of mud.

entries.text: Clean enough for washing if you take it from the lake, not the river. The river has the slaughterhouse and the tannery in it, and everything from the town. A girl who boils the river water for drinking is wiser than one who does not.

levels.8-10: It is clean enough to wash with if you take it from the lake, not the river. The river has the meat and leather shops on it, and all the town's dirt. A girl who boils river water before she drinks it is wise.

entries.text: Mrs. Kinzie, for the old families. The ministers' wives, for the churches. Mrs. Porter, who was Miss Chappel and ran the school until she married the minister last month. She has more friends than anyone and fewer enemies.

levels.8-10: Mrs. Kinzie leads the old families. The ministers' wives lead the churches. Then there is Mrs. Porter. She was Miss Chappel, and she ran the school. Last month she married the minister. She has more friends than anyone, and fewer foes.

entries.text: Pray, and send for the doctor if we can pay him, and if we cannot, ask a neighbour. There are good doctors here now: Kimberly, Egan, Maxwell at the fort. For ague, quinine; for a cough, a mustard plaster; for the summer flux, boiled water and arrowroot and a great deal of sitting up at night.

levels.8-10: We pray. We send for the doctor if we can pay him. If we can't, we ask a neighbor. There are good doctors here now, like Kimberly, Egan, and Maxwell at the fort. For chills and fever, we give quinine. For a cough, a mustard patch on the chest. For summer stomach sickness, boiled water and arrowroot, and lots of sitting up at night.

entries.text: Thirty or forty in the winter, when there is nothing else for the children to do, and a dozen in the summer, when there is everything. levels.8-10: Thirty or forty in the winter, when there is nothing else for the kids to do. A dozen in the summer, when there is everything to do. entries.text: Walk out on the lake shore on a Sunday afternoon in our best bonnets and pretend not to look at the officers from the fort. Pick strawberries on the prairie in June. Go to the singing school at the church on Thursday. In winter, skate on the river, and sleigh, and dance until the fiddler falls asleep.

levels.8-10: On Sunday afternoons we walk on the lake shore in our best bonnets. We pretend not to look at the officers from the fort. In June we pick strawberries on the prairie. On Thursday we go to singing school at the church. In winter we skate on the river, go sledding, and dance until the fiddler falls asleep.

entries.text: When the Potawatomi danced through town at the treaty, painted and singing, going down Lake Street and past the houses, and everybody standing in the doorways not sure whether to be afraid. levels.8-10: At the treaty two summers ago, the Potawatomi danced through town. They were painted and singing. They went down Lake Street and past the houses. entries.text: Every night, somewhere. Mark Beaubien plays the fiddle at the Sauganash and anybody who can dance does. There is a singing school at the Presbyterian church for the hymns. entries.text: A reel at the Sauganash, when Mark is in the mood and the floor is full and somebody's husband has to hold the candles because there is no room for a table. They say he never plays the same tune twice. They say he never stops till the last guest falls down.

entries.text: When the bell goes or somebody shouts sail, everybody runs to the river. I can tell the schooners apart by their sails. When a steamboat comes, it blows smoke and has a big wheel on the side that splashes, and all the dogs bark.

levels.8-10: When the bell rings or somebody shouts "Sail!", everybody runs to the river. I can tell the sailing ships apart by their sails. When a steamboat comes, it puffs smoke. It has a big wheel on the side that splashes. All the dogs bark.

entries.text: My grandmother speaks only French and Potawatomi, and my father French and English, and I speak all three, but my English is best because of school. At home we say grace in French. At school I am not allowed to.

levels.8-10: My grandma speaks only French and Potawatomi. My dad speaks French and English. I speak all three, but my English is best because of school. At home we pray before meals in French. At school I am not allowed to.

entries.text: Three days to go and I have four pies to bake and a dress to let out. There will be a salute from the fort, a procession, the Declaration read out by a lawyer who will take an hour about it, and a dinner at the Tremont for the gentlemen. The ladies will watch from the windows, and then we shall all dance.

levels.8-10: Three days to go, and I have four pies to bake and a dress to let out. The fort will fire its guns. There will be a parade. A lawyer will read the Declaration of Independence, and he will take an hour to do it. The men will have a dinner at the Tremont hotel. The ladies will watch from the windows. Then we will all dance.

entries.text: Potatoes, beans, peas, onions, cabbages, squash and a row of flowers for my soul, hollyhocks and pinks. A woman needs something to look at that is not mud. The Potawatomi women showed me how to plant the beans by the corn so the corn holds them up. They know more about this ground than any of us.

levels.8-10: Potatoes, beans, peas, onions, cabbages and squash. And a row of flowers for my heart, hollyhocks and pinks. A woman needs something to look at that is not mud. The Potawatomi women showed me how to plant beans next to the corn, so the corn holds them up. They know more about this ground than any of us.

entries.text: Six months, born in January in the coldest week of the winter, with the snow up to the window and the doctor stuck at the fort. My neighbour came across with a lantern and stayed till morning. That is how it is here. You have no family, so your neighbours become your family.

levels.8-10: Six months. She was born in January, in the coldest week of winter. The snow was up to the window, and the doctor was stuck at the fort. My neighbor came over with a lantern and stayed until morning. That is how it is here. You have no family, so your neighbors become your family.

entries.text: A French woman, a Laframboise, who has had seven children and knew exactly what to do. She speaks very little English and I speak no French, and we managed perfectly. She made me a broth that I would give a lot to taste again.

levels.8-10: A French woman, a Laframboise. She has had seven children, and she knew just what to do. She speaks very little English, and I speak no French. We got along just fine. She made me a soup I would give a lot to taste again.

entries.text: Hunger, mostly. Four of us on half an acre in County Cork, and the rent going up and the potatoes going black. I worked my passage to Quebec and walked to the States and followed the work: a canal in New York, a road in Ohio, and now Chicago, where they say there will be a canal that will need ten thousand of us.

levels.8-10: Hunger, mostly. Four of us lived on half an acre in County Cork, in Ireland. The rent kept going up, and the potatoes went black. I worked on a ship to pay my way to Quebec. Then I walked to the States and followed the work. I dug a canal in New York and built a road in Ohio. Now I am in Chicago. They say there will be a canal here that will need ten thousand of us.

entries.text: Saint Mary's, the little Catholic church on Lake Street, with Father St. Cyr. Wood and nails and not much of either. On a Sunday you hear Irish and French and Potawatomi and a bit of German, all saying the same prayers in different voices.

entries.text: Harbour work for the government: driving piles, filling cribs with stone, building the north pier out into the lake. It is cold work even in July. The lake comes in green over the cribs and you are wet to the waist from seven until six.

entries.text: Everything is expensive here. Broadcloth comes from New York by lake and costs twice what it does there. If you want to see him lose his temper, ask him about the Clark Street hole. If you want to see him smile, ask about his horses.

entries.text: Every week the wagons go through. Whole families, with everything they own piled up under a canvas cover, the father walking beside the oxen, the mother on the seat with the baby, the children running behind, the cow tied to the tail. They come off the schooners and buy what they need and go out across the prairie toward the Fox River and the Rock River and Iowa.

entries.text: I watch them go and I think: that was me, a year ago. And I think: one day those farms will grow wheat and send it back here to be sold. Chicago does not grow anything itself. It is a door. Everything that goes west, and everything that comes back, goes through here.

entries.text: There is not enough real money in this town. Gold and silver are scarce as diamonds. So everybody pays in paper: bank notes from Michigan and Ohio and Indiana banks, some of them good, some of them worth half, some of them printed by banks that do not exist.

entries.text: A merchant keeps a little book that tells him which notes are good this week. A man can be rich on Monday and poor on Friday because a bank in Detroit has failed. General Jackson has made war on the national bank, so now every little bank prints its own money. It is madness. But it is profitable madness, so nobody complains.

entries.text: When a steamboat comes in, the whole town knows it. You hear the whistle from far out on the lake, and then you see the smoke, and every boy in Chicago runs down to the river mouth to watch her come in past the piers.

entries.text: Fort Dearborn sits at the end of the town by the lake, its pickets and two blockhouses, and the flag over it. The soldiers come into town on their days off and spend their pay in the taverns, and the officers come to the dances.

entries.text: There are old settlers who remember the first fort, the one that was burned in the war. They say it stood in the same place. They say the people who were killed are buried somewhere along the lake shore to the south, and nobody knows exactly where. When the wind blows in from the lake on a summer night and the sand moves, sometimes, they say, you find things.

entries.text: There was no church in Chicago until two years ago. Before that the preachers held meetings wherever they could: in a tavern, in a warehouse, in the fort's carpenter shop. Now there are a handful of congregations, Presbyterian, Baptist, Methodist, Episcopal and Catholic, all trying to build churches as fast as the taverns.

entries.text: The Catholics built theirs in a few weeks, of light boards nailed together, and everybody said it would fall down. It did not. The Methodists preached on the street corner last Sunday and a man drove his cattle right through the congregation. The preacher did not stop. Neither did the cattle.

entries.text: There are more children in Chicago than benches to put them on. The first school was only three years ago, when John Watkins taught a dozen children in a little log building. Now there are several, in churches and storerooms and rented rooms, and still not enough.

entries.text: I teach thirty children in a room meant for fifteen. They are from everywhere: Vermont, Ohio, Ireland, Canada, one little French girl who speaks no English at all. I teach them reading and arithmetic and geography, and they teach me how to break up a fight between a Yankee and an Irish boy without being knocked down. Go and see Mr. Watkins. He will tell you how it was in the old days.

entries.text: When the officers at the fort hold a dance, every lady in town is invited, and there are four gentlemen for every lady, so you dance until your feet bleed. The music is a fiddle and a flute, and sometimes a soldier with a drum who cannot keep time.

entries.text: At the last dance I danced with a lieutenant, a land agent, two lawyers, a doctor, a fur trader with a scar on his face, and Mr. Beaubien, who dances like a whirlwind and sings at the same time. My husband danced with nobody, because there was nobody left. He sat by the punch bowl and talked about lots. He enjoyed himself, he says.

entries.text: My baby was born in March, in our house on Clark Street, with the snow blowing against the windows. The doctor came through the drifts on horseback and arrived just in time to say congratulations. My neighbour, Mrs. Hamilton, delivered her. She has delivered a dozen babies in this town.

He got there just in time to say congratulations! My neighbor, Mrs. Hamilton, helped the baby be born. She has helped with a dozen babies in this town.

entries.text: She is a Chicago baby. She will grow up here. She will never know a place without the lake. When she is old, I suppose, Chicago will be a great city, and she will tell her grandchildren that she remembers when it was a few wooden houses in the mud. They will not believe her.

entries.text: When we first came, a Potawatomi family camped near our house on the North Side for the summer, and the woman used to come to my door with baskets of berries to trade. I gave her flour and needles. She gave me berries and maple sugar and once a pair of moccasins for my baby that were the most beautiful thing I have ever owned.

Then she gave me the berries and would not take anything for them.

entries.text: Mrs. John Kinzie is the most interesting woman in Chicago. She came from Connecticut, married Mr. Kinzie, and went to live at a fort in the Wisconsin wilderness among the Winnebago, where her husband was the agent. She rode horseback through the forests in winter with a baby. She tells the best stories of anyone.

entries.text: Her husband's family were here at the first fort, in the old war, and his mother told her everything that happened. Mrs. Kinzie says she means to write it all down someday. I hope she does. Go and call on her if you can. She will give you tea and tell you something that will keep you awake at night.

entries.text: Twenty-three years ago, in the summer of the old war, I was nurse to the Kinzie children, a girl of French and Ottawa family. On the morning the soldiers marched out of the first fort, I sat in the Kinzies' boat at the river mouth with Mrs. Kinzie and the little ones, and we watched the column go down the shore. I will not tell you what we saw.

entries.text: Afterwards I married Jean Baptiste Beaubien, and I have raised his children and my own in this town ever since. The boy I minded in that boat, John Kinzie, is a grown man now with a business on the river. Go and find him. Ask him if he remembers the pockets I sewed into his clothes, with corn and sugar inside. He will remember.

entries.text: I brought a printing press, type, ink and paper across the lake on a schooner two years ago, and I set up the Chicago Democrat in a little building on South Water Street. The first issue came out in November of 1833, and there were so few people in town who could pay for it that I printed for the whole Northwest, by mail.

entries.text: Paper is my curse. It comes from the east, round the lakes, and when the boats stop in winter I run out, and I have had to print on whatever paper I could buy or beg. Every week I print the list of letters waiting at the post office. Go and see Mr. Hogan. Without his letters and my list, half this town would never hear from home.

entries.text: I came here in 1832 with a stock of drugs and medicines and opened the first drugstore in Chicago, in a log building at Lake Street. Quinine for the ague, calomel for the fevers, laudanum for pain, and a great many patent remedies that do more good to the seller than the buyer.

entries.text: But my real work is the Sunday school. I started it to teach the children of this town to read, and to know their Bible, in a place where there was no school and no church. There are a great many children here and not enough teachers. Go and see Mr. Watkins. He taught the first school in Chicago. He can tell you how many children there were then, and how many there are now.

entries.text: I came to Chicago at sixteen, in 1818, a clerk for the American Fur Company, in a canoe from Mackinac. The Potawatomi called me Swift Walker, because I could walk seventy-five miles in a day. I married into the Kankakee band and traded all through the Illinois country.

entries.text: In 1827, when there was a scare that the Winnebago were rising, I rode a hundred and twenty-five miles to Danville in a day and a night to bring the militia. Now I have a warehouse on the river and I pack pork and beef for the east, and I have more lots than I can walk to in a day. I knew John Kinzie the elder. His son is my friend. Go and find him. Tell him Hubbard says the canal will come.

entries.text: I came here in 1831 with a stock of goods on a schooner, and I put up one of the first frame buildings in Chicago, a store on South Water Street with my living quarters above it. Before that everything was logs.

levels.8-10: I came here in 1831 with a load of goods on a ship. I built one of the first board houses in Chicago. It was a store on South Water Street, and I lived upstairs. Before that, everything was made of logs.

entries.text: I have sold to the Potawatomi and the French, to the soldiers and the settlers, to everyone who has come through this town in four years. I have bought lots with my profits, and the lots have made me richer than the store. But I still open the shutters every morning at six, because a merchant who stops minding his store is no longer a merchant. He is a speculator. I do not want to be a speculator. Mostly.

entries.text: I taught the first school in Chicago, three years ago, in a little log building on the North Side. I had twelve pupils, and only four of them were children of Yankee families; the rest were French and Potawatomi children of the old trading families, and none of them had ever been in a school before.

entries.text: We had no books worth the name and no slates and no benches. I taught them their letters on boards with charcoal. His Sunday school taught as many children as I did.
